1 Getting Started

The TTAP Pavement Design Tool is a browser-based workspace that runs locally on your machine. No internet connection is required for calculations or report generation (only the GIS map tiles need connectivity).

Launching the tool: Unzip the distribution folder to a convenient location on your workstation. Double-click the TTAP_PDT launcher file (batch file on Windows, shell script on macOS). This starts a lightweight local server and opens the application in your default browser at http://localhost:8080.

System requirements: You need Python 3 installed on your machine. macOS ships with Python pre-installed. On Windows, download the latest Python 3 from python.org and ensure it is added to your system PATH during installation. The tool works in any modern browser — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari.

The templates/ folder included in the distribution contains pre-formatted Excel input templates for FWD data, traffic counts, and investigation records. Use these templates to ensure your data imports correctly.

Tip
Your work is auto-saved to browser local storage every 60 seconds. For additional safety, use the JSON export function regularly — particularly before closing your browser or switching machines.
2 Dashboard

The Dashboard is the landing page of the tool. It provides an overview of your current project status including step completion percentages, validation summary counts (blockers, warnings, passes), and quick-action buttons for common tasks.

Project statistics: The top panel shows the number of completed steps, the current design ESA (if traffic data has been entered), and the overall validation status. Red blockers must be resolved before generating a compliant report.

Loading example projects: Three pre-loaded example projects are available for training and reference — SH1 Utiku South, SH54 Kimbolton, and SH3 Kai-Iwi. These contain real Manawatu-Whanganui corridor data and demonstrate a complete workflow from project setup through to structural analysis. Click any example to load it immediately.

Input templates: The Dashboard provides download links for standardised Excel input templates. Use the FWD template for deflection bowl data and the traffic template for count station records. These templates ensure column headers and units match the import parser.

Tip
Load the SH1 Utiku South example first and walk through each step to familiarise yourself with the interface before starting your own project.
3 Project Setup

Project Setup captures the administrative and classification data that frames the entire design. All fields on this step feed into the final NZTA report header and are referenced by validation rules throughout the tool.

Project identification: Enter the project name, Waka Kotahi contract number, region (defaults to Manawatu-Whanganui), corridor name, and state highway route number. These appear on every page of the generated report.

Route position extents: Specify the start and end RP (Route Position) values in kilometres. The tool uses these to define the section length and to position FWD test points on the GIS map.

ONRC category: Select the One Network Road Classification for the corridor. This determines minimum design reliability, surfacing expectations, and informs the treatment scoring algorithm. Categories range from National (high volume state highway) through to Access (low volume local road).

Design parameters: Set the design life in years (typically 25 for state highways) and the target reliability level (commonly 90% or 95% for ONRC Primary Collector and above). Enter the Weighted Mean Annual Pavement Temperature (WMAPT) for the project location — this is used to temperature-adjust asphalt modulus values. For the Manawatu-Whanganui region, WMAPT is typically 17–19°C.

Important
ONRC category and design life cannot be changed after structural analysis has been run without resetting downstream calculations. Set these values carefully at the outset.
4 GIS & Mapping

The GIS step provides an interactive map for visualising your project corridor, FWD test locations, and pavement condition data spatially. It uses LINZ (Land Information New Zealand) basemap tiles for accurate NZ topographic and aerial context.

Basemap layers: Five basemap options are available — Topo (topographic), Aerial (satellite imagery), Streets, Terrain (hillshade), and Hybrid (aerial with labels). Toggle between them using the layer control in the top-right corner of the map.

Road alignment: When RP extents and corridor coordinates are defined, the tool displays the road alignment as a polyline on the map. You can zoom and pan to inspect the section in detail.

FWD markers: If FWD deflection data has been uploaded in the Investigation step, each test point appears as a marker on the map at its RP location. Click a marker to see the deflection bowl summary for that station.

Note
Map tiles require an active internet connection to load. The rest of the tool works fully offline — if you are working without connectivity, the map area will appear blank but all other functionality remains available.
5 Traffic Basis

The Traffic Basis step defines the traffic loading that the pavement must be designed to carry. This is the primary input to the structural design — an incorrect ESA estimate will invalidate the entire analysis.

Key inputs: Enter the current AADT (Annual Average Daily Traffic), HCV percentage (Heavy Commercial Vehicles as a proportion of total traffic), and select the appropriate TLD class (Traffic Load Distribution) from the seven standard classes. TLD class defines the axle load spectrum and has a significant impact on ESA.

Growth and design life: Specify the traffic growth rate (percent per annum) and confirm the design life (carried forward from Project Setup). The tool applies compound growth to calculate cumulative traffic over the design period.

ESA calculation: The design ESA (Equivalent Standard Axles) is calculated automatically from your inputs using the NZ Supplement methodology. The result is displayed prominently and categorised by magnitude. You can also adjust the ESA/HVAG ratio if project-specific axle load data suggests a non-standard value.

Data source: Document the source of your traffic data (e.g., RAMM TMS site number, manual count dates) in the notes field. This is included in the report and is a common NZTA review query.

Tip
Always cross-check your calculated ESA against the RAMM traffic loading estimate for the corridor. Significant discrepancies should be investigated before proceeding to structural design.
6 Investigation & Evidence

This step collates the field investigation data and evidence that underpins your design decisions. The tool accepts multiple file types and provides summary statistics for FWD deflection data.

Uploading evidence: Click the upload area or drag files to attach investigation evidence. Supported formats include Excel (.xlsx), CSV, PDF reports, and image files (JPG, PNG) for condition photos. Each uploaded file is tagged with a category (FWD, DCP, test pit, visual assessment, lab results).

FWD deflection data: When FWD data is uploaded using the standard template, the tool parses the deflection bowls and displays summary statistics — mean, standard deviation, and characteristic d0 values by chainage. These statistics inform the subgrade modulus estimation used in structural analysis.

Visual assessment: Record walkover observations including surface distress types, severity, and extent. The visual assessment narrative is included in the failure mode analysis and the final report.

Use the Download FWD Template button to obtain the standardised spreadsheet format. The template includes column headers for station RP, d0 through d6 deflections (microns), surface temperature, and pavement temperature — matching the standard NZ FWD reporting format.

Important
FWD deflections must be in microns and normalised to a 40 kN load. The import parser expects this standard. Raw unnormalised data will produce incorrect modulus estimates.
7 Failure Mode Analysis

Failure Mode Analysis is a core NZTA requirement. You must identify and document the mechanisms driving pavement deterioration on your corridor before selecting a treatment. The tool provides all 13 NZTA-defined failure modes.

Selecting failure modes: Review each of the 13 modes (e.g., structural deformation, shear failure, moisture damage, age hardening, reflective cracking) and tick those that are applicable to your project. For each selected mode, designate whether it is the primary mode or a contributing mode.

Evidence narrative: For each selected failure mode, enter a brief evidence narrative explaining why you believe this mode is active. Reference specific investigation findings — FWD deflection trends, test pit observations, or surface distress patterns. This narrative feeds directly into the report.

Confidence rating: Assign a confidence level (High, Medium, Low) to each failure mode assessment. Low confidence modes flag automatically in the QA validation step as items requiring additional investigation or peer review.

Tip
The primary failure mode determines the treatment strategy. If you are uncertain, select "Medium" confidence and add a QA comment noting that further investigation or peer review is needed. NZTA reviewers will query failure mode assessments that lack supporting evidence.
8 Treatment Options

The Treatment Options step generates and compares rehabilitation strategies based on your failure mode assessment, traffic loading, and pavement condition. The tool scores each option across five weighted criteria.

Option cards: The tool generates treatment options as scored cards. Each card shows the treatment type (e.g., mill and replace AC, stabilisation, overlay, reconstruction), a brief description, and the composite score. Select your preferred option to carry forward into structural analysis.

Score components: Each option is scored on five criteria: structural adequacy (does it address the primary failure mode?), drainage improvement (does it resolve moisture-related issues?), economic value (cost-effectiveness over the design life), constructability (traffic management complexity, material availability), and sustainability (resource efficiency, carbon footprint).

The scoring algorithm uses the 14-type treatment matrix and considers your specific ONRC category, ESA range, and failure mode combination to rank options. You can override the tool's recommendation if engineering judgement warrants a different approach — document your reasoning in the notes field.

Note
The treatment scoring algorithm has been calibrated for Manawatu-Whanganui conditions (material availability, climate, contractor capability). If you are using the tool outside this region, treat the scores as indicative only and apply local engineering judgement.
9 Structural Analysis

Structural Analysis is the engineering core of the tool. It implements an Austroads mechanistic-empirical (M-E) design approach using Odemark equivalent thickness theory and Boussinesq elastic analysis, calibrated to NZ conditions.

Layer stack entry: Build your pavement structure from top down. For each layer, select a material from the Material Library (13 NZ-standard materials including AC14 asphalt, M/4 AP40 basecourse, foam bitumen stabilised, cement-treated, and subgrade types) and specify the layer thickness in millimetres. The subgrade is always the bottom layer with a nominal thickness of 9999 mm.

Material Library: Each material in the library has a pre-defined modulus (MPa), Poisson's ratio, and structural coefficient. For asphalt layers, the reference modulus is automatically adjusted for the project WMAPT using the temperature-modulus relationship. You can override individual modulus values if you have project-specific test data (e.g., from laboratory resilient modulus testing).

Analysis results: The tool calculates three damage criteria simultaneously:

  • Subgrade strain criterion: Vertical compressive strain at the top of the subgrade, converted to allowable load repetitions via the Austroads subgrade fatigue relationship N = (9300/microstrain)^7.14.
  • Asphalt fatigue criterion: Horizontal tensile strain at the base of the asphalt layer, converted to allowable repetitions via the Asphalt Institute fatigue formula.
  • Bound layer fatigue: For cement-stabilised or foam bitumen layers, the bound fatigue criterion N = (K/microstrain)^12 is applied.

CDF summary: The Cumulative Damage Factor (CDF = design ESA / allowable repetitions) is displayed for each active criterion. A CDF below 1.0 is a PASS (the pavement has sufficient life). The summary banner shows green for PASS and red for FAIL, with the governing criterion highlighted.

Important
This tool uses a simplified Boussinesq model for rapid optioneering. For final detailed design submissions, verify critical results against CIRCLY 7.0, particularly for thin asphalt pavements on weak subgrades (CBR 3–5) where the simplified model tends to overestimate strain.
10 Drainage & Geometry

Drainage and geometry parameters influence pavement performance and are required fields in the NZTA design report. Moisture is the single largest contributor to premature pavement failure in the Manawatu-Whanganui region.

Drainage type: Select the subsurface drainage arrangement — options include no subsoil drainage, edge drains, full-width subsoil system, or deep drainage. The drainage type affects the moisture condition assumption used in subgrade modulus estimation.

Crossfall and geometry: Enter the existing and proposed crossfall (%), carriageway width, shoulder width, and batter slopes. These parameters are reported in the design documentation and inform constructability assessment.

Outlet condition: Record the condition of drainage outlets (functioning, partially blocked, fully blocked). Poor outlet condition is a common finding on state highway rehabilitation projects and should be flagged as a pre-treatment maintenance item.

Tip
If drainage data is incomplete, enter what you have and flag the gaps in QA comments. Partial drainage data is better than none — NZTA reviewers expect to see drainage considered even when full assessment data is not yet available.
11 Surfacing Design

Surfacing Design specifies the wearing course that protects the structural pavement and provides skid resistance and waterproofing. This step covers chip seal and asphaltic surfacing options consistent with NZTA M/10 and T/3 specifications.

Seal type: Select from nine standard seal types including single coat, two coat, racked-in, geotextile SAM/SAMI, Cape seal, and asphaltic concrete surfacing. The seal type should be compatible with the traffic loading (ESA) and ONRC category.

Chip and binder specification: Specify the aggregate chip size (Grade 2, 3, 4, or 5), aggregate source, and binder type (80/100 pen bitumen, PMB, emulsion). For polymer-modified binders, indicate the PMB grade and target application rate.

Stress and modification factors: Enter the stress factor for the surfacing location (influenced by gradient, curvature, intersection proximity) and any polymer modification requirements. High-stress sites on state highways typically require PMB surfacing.

Tip
Surfacing design should be consistent with the Network Outcomes Contract surfacing standards for the corridor. Check the current NOC surfacing specification before finalising the seal type and aggregate source.
12 QA & Validation

The QA & Validation step runs 22 automated business rules across all project data and presents the results as a structured validation panel. This is your pre-submission quality gate.

Validation categories: Issues are classified as Blockers (must be resolved — shown in red), Warnings (should be reviewed — shown in amber), and Passes (compliant — shown in green). The tool checks for missing mandatory fields, inconsistent parameters (e.g., ESA outside expected range for the ONRC category), and incomplete failure mode documentation.

Completeness checklist: A 14-item checklist mirrors the NZTA submission requirements. Each item shows whether the corresponding data has been entered and validated. All 14 items must show green before the design can be considered submission-ready.

QA review comments: Add reviewer comments and sign-off notes directly in the tool. These are timestamped and included in the report appendix. Use this for internal TTAP peer review documentation.

Note
The tool will allow you to generate a report even with unresolved blockers, but the report will display a prominent "DRAFT — VALIDATION INCOMPLETE" watermark. Resolve all blockers before issuing a report for NZTA submission.
13 Outputs & Reports

The Outputs step generates a formatted HTML report that follows the NZTA Pavement Design Strawman structure (Appendix 5). The report is designed to be directly printable as a PDF for submission.

Report generation: Click "Generate Report" to open the formatted report in a new browser window. The report pulls all data from the current project state and assembles it into 10 structured sections covering project description, traffic assessment, investigation summary, failure mode analysis, treatment selection, structural design, surfacing, drainage, QA summary, and appendices.

Report structure: The 10 report sections are:

  1. Project Description & Scope
  2. Traffic Assessment
  3. Pavement Investigation Summary
  4. Failure Mode Assessment
  5. Treatment Option Analysis
  6. Structural Pavement Design
  7. Surfacing Design
  8. Drainage & Geometry
  9. Quality Assurance Summary
  10. Appendices (calculation details, data tables)

Print to PDF: Use your browser's print function (Ctrl+P or Cmd+P) from the report window to save as PDF. The report CSS is optimised for A4 printing with correct margins, page breaks, and TTAP branding.

Project backup: The JSON export/import function allows you to save the complete project state as a file and restore it later or transfer it to another machine. Use "Export Project JSON" to download and "Import Project JSON" to restore. The import includes schema validation to detect corrupted or incompatible files.

Tip
Always export a JSON backup before generating the final report. This preserves the exact project state that produced the report and provides an audit trail if NZTA requests clarification on any design parameters.
